zumir

Overview

A loop over a numeric vector is often the slow part of an R program. The usual fix is to rewrite it in C or C++, and that needs a toolchain: Rtools on Windows, the Xcode command-line tools on macOS, gcc elsewhere. Locked-down laptops, Shiny servers and slim containers often have none.

zumir brings MIR, Vladimir Makarov’s small just-in-time compiler, to R. It is vendored, so a numeric R function or a short C function becomes native code from R itself, with nothing else installed.

  • No toolchain. mir_compile() compiles an R function, and cfunction() a C function, in memory, in milliseconds.
  • R’s answers, or an error. A function compiled by mir_compile() returns what R returns, every number bit for bit. Where matching R would be costly, it refuses, and names the construct.
  • The same C everywhere. cfunction() reads no system header and links only the C maths library and a few memory and string functions, so a source behaves the same on every machine.
  • MIR never ends your session. A compile error, a bad module, or MIR running out of memory becomes an R condition you can catch.
  • A compiler for packages too. Packages that generate code link to zumir’s versioned C interface (LinkingTo: zumir) and get native function pointers back.

Installation

zumir is not on CRAN yet. Install the development version from GitHub with:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("pedrobtz/zumir")

Installing it from source needs a C compiler once; using it never does.

Usage 

library(zumir)

Here is a cumulative sum written as an R loop. mir_compile() turns it into native code with the same arguments.

csum_r <- function(x) {
  y <- numeric(length(x))
  acc <- 0
  for (i in seq_along(x)) {
    acc <- acc + x[i]
    y[i] <- acc
  }
  y
}
csum <- mir_compile(csum_r)
csum(c(1, 2, 3, 4))
#> [1]  1  3  6 10

It answers as R does, missing values included.

x <- c(1, 2, NA, 4)
csum(x)
#> [1]  1  3 NA NA
identical(csum(x), csum_r(x))
#> [1] TRUE

What it cannot match it refuses when it compiles, never by giving another answer. Here R would return a character vector.

mir_compile(function(x) paste(x))
#> Error:
#> ! mir_compile(): `paste` is not in the subset in `paste(x)`.

When an R loop is not enough, cfunction() compiles one C function. An argument named in out is allocated for the call and returned, and n receives the inputs’ length.

dot <- cfunction("
  double dot(int n, const double *x, const double *y) {
    double s = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) s += x[i] * y[i];
    return s;
  }", n = "n")
dot(x = c(1, 2, 3), y = c(4, 5, 6))
#> [1] 32

On a loop over a million doubles, mir_compile()’s code ran about 35 times faster than R’s byte-compiled function, and within 1.3 times of cfunction()’s. If generated code fails the check zumir runs when it loads, both fall back to MIR’s interpreter, which gives the same answers more slowly. Where MIR has no code generator for the processor, or the system refuses memory that is both writable and executable, nothing can be compiled. zumir_tier() says which of these holds in this session.

zumir_tier()
#> [1] "native"

Acknowledgements

zumir is built on MIR by Vladimir Makarov: its generator, interpreter and c2mir C compiler, from a fork that carries zumir’s patches (pedrobtz/mir). cfunction() is checked against MIR’s own c-tests corpus, and mir_compile() against R itself.
